opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've gone back and forth on quite a bit over the years.

Early on, honestly, I was somewhat skeptical about how essential tactile sensing really was. A lot of my work, especially on locomotion, showed that you could get remarkably far with proprioception alone, meaning joint encoders, motor currents, and an IMU. A legged robot can "feel" the ground through its own body without dedicated touch sensors on its feet. And in manipulation, vision was improving so quickly that it seemed like cameras plus good learned policies might cover most of what we needed. Tactile sensors at the time were also fragile, expensive, hard to calibrate, and they produced data that was difficult to simulate, which made them a poor fit for the sim-to-real pipelines we relied on.

As the hardware matured, especially as we moved toward dexterous hands and more contact-rich tasks, my view shifted. Once a hand is closed around an object, the cameras simply can't see what's happening at the contact points. Occlusion is a fundamental problem, not something better vision models will solve. Tasks like inserting a plug, sliding a card out of a wallet, or adjusting your grip on a slippery cup depend on information about force, slip, and contact geometry that you can only get from touch. Humans make this obvious: when your fingertips are numb from cold, even simple manipulation becomes clumsy, though your eyes work fine.

The sensors themselves have also gotten much better. Vision-based tactile sensors, more robust skins, and cheaper, more durable designs make it realistic to put touch on a robot that runs for hours instead of minutes. So the bottleneck has moved from "is this hardware usable?" to "how do we learn from this data at scale?"

So today I'd say tactile sensing isn't strictly necessary for every task, since many things can be done with vision and proprioception. But for the kind of fine, robust, general-purpose dexterity we ultimately want, I now think it's very hard to get there without touch. The open challenge is less the sensor and more the data and the learning: how we collect large tactile datasets, how we simulate touch well enough, and how we fuse it with vision and language in a single model.

r002.rationale: It describes camera occlusion at contact points, but says nothing about scissors, their loops, or vision failing to guide when the hand should open or close.

r003.rationale: It says the earlier tactile sensors were fragile, expensive, hard to calibrate, and difficult to simulate, framing them as a poor fit for the hardware and pipelines available then.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, my view on this has flipped a couple of times.

Early on, when I was doing a lot of the legged locomotion work, I was skeptical that touch sensing mattered much. We had proprioception, we had joint encoders, motor currents, IMUs, and with sim-to-real and reinforcement learning you could get a quadruped walking over pretty rough terrain without a single dedicated tactile sensor on the foot. The policy could infer contact from the dynamics. So my instinct was that tactile was a nice-to-have, and that vision plus proprioception plus learning would carry most of the load.

What changed my mind was moving from locomotion to manipulation. Walking is forgiving. You have a big body, big contact forces, and the physics kind of tells you what's happening. Manipulation isn't like that. The moment you try to grasp something deformable, or something slippery, or do an in-hand reorientation, the camera just can't see what you need. The fingers occlude the object, the forces are tiny, and the difference between a stable grasp and a drop is a few millimeters of slip you simply cannot observe from the outside. That's where I realized the gap wasn't a software gap. Learning couldn't fill it because the information literally wasn't entering the system.

And then the hardware side shifted too. For a long time tactile sensors were expensive, fragile, and gave you noisy, hard-to-interpret signals, so even if you wanted touch you'd end up fighting the sensor more than using it. Over the last few years that's improved a lot. Vision-based tactile sensors like GelSight-style skins got cheaper and more robust, and you can now put dense touch on a hand at a cost that's reasonable. Once the data gets cleaner and denser, it fits naturally into the same learning pipelines we use for vision, which is a big deal. The sensor stops being a special case and becomes just another modality for the model.

So where I've landed is something like this. For gross motion, touch is still optional, and I'd rather spend the effort on good control and simulation. For dexterous manipulation, the kind of thing we want general-purpose robots to do in homes, I now think tactile sensing is close to necessary, not because it's elegant, but because without it you're asking the robot to do a task blindfolded in exactly the moments that matter most. The interesting open question for me now is less whether we need it and more how to get it into simulation well enough that we can train on it at scale, because that's the part of the pipeline that's still immature.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss scissors, their loops, or vision failing to indicate when to open or close the hand.

r003.rationale: It says earlier tactile sensors were expensive, fragile, noisy, and difficult to use, explaining that these hardware limitations made touch difficult to adopt.

astra-6.text:
My view has shifted from thinking tactile sensing is a useful addition to thinking it’s a very important part of dexterous manipulation. When the hardware is limited—say, a simple gripper picking up an object—you can get surprisingly far with vision and a fairly simple control strategy. But as hands become more capable, with more fingers and more degrees of freedom, you need richer feedback to take advantage of that capability.

Vision can tell you where an object is, but once you make contact, a lot of what matters becomes difficult to see. Is the object slipping? How much pressure are you applying? Has a finger actually established contact? Those questions become especially important when you’re moving an object within the hand or handling something delicate.

So I think better hardware actually makes the need for touch more apparent. The challenge is to make that sensing reliable and to build learning and control systems that can use it effectively.

sol-6.1.text:
My view has shifted from thinking of tactile sensing as a useful addition to thinking of it as a very important part of making robots work reliably in the real world. When you’re focused on locomotion, you can get surprisingly far with joint encoders, an IMU, and estimates of contact forces. That can make it seem like touch is optional.

But as the hardware becomes more capable, especially when you start working on dexterous manipulation, the limitations become much clearer. A camera can tell you where an object is, but once your fingers make contact, you need to know what’s happening at that contact. Is the object slipping? Are you applying too much force? Have you actually established a stable grasp? Some of that information is very difficult to get from vision alone, especially because the hand itself blocks the view.

So I increasingly see hardware and sensing as things that have to develop together. Having more joints and more dexterity creates opportunities, but you need the sensory feedback to take advantage of them. The challenge is making tactile sensors robust and integrating their signals into learning and control so that the robot can actually use that information.
